pages.title: Basics
pages.body:
# Basics

This document contains some foundational information on how [computers](/en/block/computer) work. This does not necessarily mean that this information is easy reading. Basic here means the general concepts in use.

## Architecture

Computers run on a single-core, general purpose RISC-V architecture. This means they have 64-bit registers and support floating point operations. This makes it possible to boot a modern Linux kernel on them.

### Native Devices

Native devices connected to computers are memory-mapped devices. This means they are mapped to some area in physical memory. Computers use regular Linux drivers to interact with them.

What devices are available, and where those devices live, is communicated to the software running on the computer using a flattened device tree. This data structure may contain additional information on the system in general. In particular, it also stores the size of the installed [memory](/en/item/memory). Since this data structure gets copied during boot, it cannot be updated later on. This is the reason computers must be rebooted when changes to native devices, such as the [network interface card](/en/item/network_interface_card), are made. Devices for which this is the case will typically have a corresponding note in their tooltip.

### HLAPI Devices

The other type of device are high level API devices, sometimes also called RPC devices. These devices use a single controller which communicates with the computers via single serial device. This controller device is present in all computers, and takes care of collecting messages from multiple devices, and dispatching messages to devices. The protocol this controller uses is a simple JSON message based protocol. The `devices` Lua library provided with the default Linux library wraps around the serial device used to connect to this controller. As such, using the `devices` library whenever using a HLAPI device, such as the [redstone interface block](/en/block/redstone_interface), is *strongly* recommended.

Due to the nature of the employed protocol, data rate is rather limited. Most devices therefore usually only provide comparatively simple APIs which do not require sending large amounts of data either way.

## Configuration

Computers can be configured to some degree. The amount of memory, extra storage in the form of [hard drives](/en/item/hard_drive) and most importantly, which cards to install, are largely up to the user. Install a CPU as well as RAM; 32 MiB is a practical starting point for the bundled Linux. See [getting started](/en/getting_started).

Most components contribute to the overall energy consumption of a computer. To conserve energy, choosing only the necessary components is essential.

## Linux

The default Linux distribution contains some basic command line tools, and the ability to write and run Lua programs. For an overview of how to interact with HLAPI devices using Lua, please see the [scripting](/en/scripting) manual entry.

Native devices use regular Linux drivers. For example, whole disks appear as */dev/vda*, */dev/vdb* and so on; partitions, when present, add a number such as */dev/vda1*. The built-in root disk also occupies a device name. Inspect */proc/partitions* before formatting an extra disk.

Computers provide two hardware clock (RTC) devices. The first one counts time in a scale most users will think in. It is used by default, for example by command line tools like *date* and *time*. The second one measures time as it works in the world the computer runs in. To obtain the current world time, use *hwclock -f /dev/rtc1*.

---

`oc2r:bus_cable`

The bus cable connects [bus interfaces](/en/block/bus_interface) to a computer.

Placed cables may be hidden by placing any regular decorative block on them. Remove a facade block by using a [wrench](/en/item/wrench) on it.

pages.title: Bus Interface
pages.body:
# Bus Interface

`oc2r:bus_interface`

Bus interfaces connect external devices to [computers](/en/block/computer). This includes explicit device blocks, such as the [redstone interface](/en/block/redstone_interface). Some generic functionality blocks of blocks is also available, such as information on energy storage.

It is possible to configure an explicit name for a bus interface using a [wrench](/en/item/wrench). This is useful when attaching multiple devices of the same type to a computer: when searching devices by type name (*devices:find(typeName)*), these custom names will also work.

Note that [computers](/en/block/computer) must also be explicitly connected to a [bus](/en/block/bus_cable) with a bus connector.

pages.title: Charger
pages.body:
# Charger
`oc2r:charger`

The charger transfers energy from a connected power source to energy consumers on top of it.

The employed wireless energy transfer mechanism supports any consumer accepting RF energy. In particular, blocks and entities, as well as items in regular item containers (such as blocks and entities) will be charged.

This device is particularly useful to recharge [robots](/en/item/robot) or energy consuming devices in your inventory.

pages.title: Computer
pages.body: # Computer `oc2r:computer` Computers provide a basis for building hardware capable of running an operating system or low-level software. *A powered computer with a connected monitor, running OnyxOS in this demonstration. (Minecraft 26.1.2)* Read the [quickstart guide](/en/getting_started) for a short explanation on how to get a working computer. ### Configuration Configure the components in a computer in its inventory screen. To access this screen, either open the computer with a [wrench](/en/item/wrench), or switch to the inventory screen using the toggle button to the left of the terminal screen. ### Connectivity To connect external devices to a computer, use [bus interfaces](/en/block/bus_interface) and [bus cables](/en/block/bus_cable). Note that computers must be explicitly connected to a bus with a bus interface. ### Energy Usually, computers will require energy to run. Most modern energy generators producing RF energy should be compatible. Computers have a small built-in energy storage. However, this will usually not be sufficient to keep the machine running for any prolonged amount of time. A [CPU](/en/item/cpu), RAM and valid firmware are required. A [GPU](/en/item/gpu) is needed for monitors, while the built-in terminal works without one. ## In game Actual Minecraft 26.1.2 screenshots from the OC2R demonstration world. *The demonstration computer inventory: four 16 MiB memory modules, a GPU and OnyxOS firmware. This is an example configuration, not a minimum requirement. (Minecraft 26.1.2)* ## Crafting recipes - [Computer](/en/recipes#recipe-computer) --- [OC2R source](https://github.com/DivByDiamond/OC2R/blob/39eb8109e2e38fdb047af98d8e6f7ded0194f498/src/main/resources/assets/oc2r/doc/en_us/block/computer.md) · `39eb8109e2e3`

pages.title: GPS tower
pages.body:
# GPS tower
`oc2r:gps_tower`

The tower reports its base position and dimension. Relative mode adds explicitly paired radio networks whose stations report offsets from a selected reference.

Place it on a solid foundation with five blocks of vertical clearance. Connect its base to the computer's device bus. RPC device name: `gps_tower`.

## Default mode

```lua
local gps = assert(require("devices"):find("gps_tower"))
local p = gps:getPosition()
print(p[1], p[2], p[3])
print(gps:getDimension())
```

By default the result is the base's world X, Y, Z. A damaged tower raises an error. `isAssembled()` checks the structure.

## Relative mode

:::note
The radio network and relative-coordinate configuration described here are local development changes after the baseline source revision linked below. Published builds may not include them.
:::

Enable `gameplay.relative_coordinates` in the common OC2R config. `gameplay.gps_tower_range` controls the maximum straight-line 3D hop distance, defaulting to 45 blocks.

Call `setAsReference()` on the first tower and read `getNetworkId()`. At additional towers, pass that ID to `joinNetwork(id)`. A network may have only one reference; its position is `(0, 0, 0)`.

`hasSignal()` checks for a route to the reference. Without a route, `getPosition()` raises an error rather than returning world XYZ. Other networks cannot relay the signal. Unloaded stations continue using the persisted topology. Breaking a station removes it.

To move the origin, first call `clearReference()` on the old reference, then select another member. Update saved waypoints after changing the origin.

The tower does not locate players or add a GPS receiver to a [robot](/en/item/robot). Robot positions remain local.

[Full setup and method reference](https://wiki.loki-code.dev/en/reference/gps-networks).

<!-- wiki-recipes -->
## Crafting recipes

- [Positioning Tower](/en/recipes#recipe-gps_tower)
<!-- /wiki-recipes -->

# Internet Gateway
`oc2r:internet_gateway`

The gateway exposes the host-backed Internet adapter to the device network. Connect it with network connectors and cables, not a device-bus cable. Internet access must be enabled by the server administrator, and destination/session restrictions still apply.

It forwards Ethernet frames; it is not an automatic DHCP server. See the [Internet card](/en/item/internet_card) for point-to-point setup requirements and [networking](/en/networking) for local network setup.

pages.title: Keyboard
pages.body:
# Keyboard

`oc2r:keyboard`

The keyboard allows key presses to be picked up by [computers](/en/block/computer). Its primary use-case is in combination with a [projector](/en/block/projector), when using a Linux system.

When using the default Linux distribution, this device will provide events via the *evdev* system. To use its input this without additional configuration, use a [projector](/en/block/projector). The keyboard input will be sent to the terminal session displayed there.

Note that the only face of the keyboard device large enough to fit a bus interface is at the bottom. Keyboards may be placed anywhere, as long as they're connected to the computer via a bus.

To start typing on a keyboard, simply interact with it. Experienced typists will find they do not need to look at the keys while typing (you can still look around while using the keyboard). Interact again to stop using the keyboard.

Computers *have to be shut down* before installing or removing this component. Installing it while the computer is running will have no effect, removing it may lead to system errors.

<!-- wiki-recipes -->
## Crafting recipes

- [Keyboard](/en/recipes#recipe-keyboard)
<!-- /wiki-recipes -->

pages.title: Machine interface
pages.body:
# Machine interface

The machine interface gives programs access to the machine facing its connector. Attach it to the computer's device bus. The RPC device name is `machine_interface`. See its [crafting recipe](/en/recipes#recipe-machine_interface).

```lua
local m = assert(require("devices"):find("machine_interface"))
print(m:getTargetBlock())
print(m:getTargetSlotCount())
```

Access follows the target machine's sided item, fluid and energy handlers. An unsupported handler raises an error.

## Items

The menu has 18 regular buffer slots, numbered 0–17. Internal slot 18 retains items that could not be returned during a transfer. Call `recoverItems()` before attempting more transfers when recovery is pending.

| Method | Purpose |
|---|---|
| `getTargetSlotCount()` | Target slot count |
| `getTargetItem(slot)` | Inspect a target slot |
| `getBufferItem(slot)` | Inspect a buffer slot |
| `pushItems(bufferSlot, targetSlot, amount)` | Buffer to target |
| `pullItems(targetSlot, bufferSlot, amount)` | Target to buffer |
| `recoverItems()` | Recover retained transfer items |

Transfers return actual item counts. Slot indices start at zero.

## Fluids and energy

`getEnergyStored()` and `getFluidStored()` inspect local buffers. Use `getTargetEnergyStored()`, `getTargetTankCount()` and `getTargetFluid(tank)` for the attached machine.

`pullEnergy(amount)` and `pullFluid(amount)` move resources from the target into the buffer. `pushEnergy(amount)` and `pushFluid(amount)` move them to the target. Check returned amounts. `recoverFluid()` handles retained fluid.

## State and settings

`getTargetBlock()` reports the block ID. `getTargetState()` reports block-state properties. Supported Create machines also expose `getSettings()` and `setSetting(id, value)`. The interface exposes supported settings rather than arbitrary target NBT. Unsupported settings APIs raise an error.

<!-- wiki-recipes -->
## Crafting recipes

- [Machine Interface](/en/recipes#recipe-machine_interface)
<!-- /wiki-recipes -->

pages.title: Media Station
pages.body:
# Media Station
`oc2r:media_station`

The media station combines a floppy drive and a flash/HDD programmer. Its upper bay accepts a floppy; its lower bay accepts flash memory or an HDD. A single rear bus port exposes both as independent block devices.

Insert media using the held item. Sneak-use the upper half to eject the floppy or the lower half to eject flash/HDD media. Normal use opens the firmware/image writer. Programming locks the lower bay; shut down a computer that has mounted that medium before programming it locally.

Unmount media in the guest before ejecting it. Identify guest block devices in */proc/partitions*. The old standalone drive and programmer have been removed; use the media station for both functions.

<!-- wiki-recipes -->
## Crafting recipes

- [Media Station](/en/recipes#recipe-media_station)
<!-- /wiki-recipes -->

pages.title: Monitor
pages.body: # Monitor `oc2r:monitor` The monitor, like the projector, provides a framebuffer device to [computers](/en/block/computer). Its resolution is selected by the installed [GPU](/en/item/gpu): 320x200, 640x400, 1024x768 or 1920x1080. Without a GPU it stays dark. The framebuffer uses RGB565 (5 red, 6 green and 5 blue bits). *Two separate monitors attached to one computer show independent framebuffers at the same time: telemetry and the ONYX OS display. (Minecraft 26.1.2)* Monitors need to be powered directly to function. The device bus cannot provide enough energy on its own. When insufficiently powered, this is indicated by a red error text on the screen. On a Linux system, monitors will typically appear as */dev/fbX* devices. To send data to the framebuffer, it is possible to write to these devices. For example, to clear a framebuffer one might pipe zeros to the device like so: *cat /dev/zero > /dev/fb0*. The monitor provides a built-in keyboard for usage with the default Linux distro, this feature may be interrupted by having another keyboard device connected to the same computer. Computers *have to be shut down* before installing or removing this component. Installing it while the computer is running will have no effect, removing it may lead to system errors. ## Multiblock Monitors Monitors can be combined into larger screens by placing additional monitor blocks next to an existing monitor (similar to OpenComputers 1.12.2). When two monitors with the same facing are placed adjacent to each other, they automatically merge into a single larger display. The multiblock can be grown up to 8 blocks wide and 8 blocks tall. The framebuffer content at the GPU resolution is scaled to fill the entire multiblock area, so a 2x2 monitor displays the same image as a 1x1 monitor but four times larger. Only one of the blocks in a multiblock (the master) hosts the actual device bus connection and framebuffer device — the others are inert casing blocks. Interacting with any block of the multiblock (right-click, shift-right-click) is redirected to the master. Breaking any block of the multiblock with a pickaxe or wrench will break the entire multiblock and drop one monitor item per block at the broken position. ## In game Actual Minecraft 26.1.2 screenshots from the OC2R demonstration world. *A 3×2 multiblock monitor displaying the OnyxOS console. This is one large screen, not several independent displays. (Minecraft 26.1.2)* --- [OC2R source](https://github.com/DivByDiamond/OC2R/blob/39eb8109e2e38fdb047af98d8e6f7ded0194f498/src/main/resources/assets/oc2r/doc/en_us/block/monitor.md) · `39eb8109e2e3`

pages.title: Network Connector
pages.body:
# Network Connector
`oc2r:network_connector`

The network connector is a fundamental part for building a network connecting different [computers](/en/block/computer). Use [network cables](/en/item/network_cable) to connect connectors with each other.

Each connector will represent one "hop" for relayed packets. Packets may only travel a limited number of hops before they are dropped.

Note that each connector only supports up to two attached network cables. Chain multiple connectors to increase the range that can be spanned.

Create a simple multi-computer network by chaining the connectors attached to the computers. To create a mesh network, use a [network hub](/en/block/network_hub). The hub connects all attached connectors with each other.

<!-- wiki-recipes -->

# Network Hub
`oc2r:network_hub`

The network hub connects multiple [network connectors](/en/block/network_connector) with each other. It forwards any packet arriving at any attached connector to all other attached connectors. This forwarding operation will consume one hop, reducing the packet's time to live.

pages.title: Projector
pages.body: # Projector `oc2r:projector` The projector provides a framebuffer device to [computers](/en/block/computer). They have a resolution of 640 by 480 pixels, with the color format r5g6b5: 5 bits for the red color component, 6 bits for the green color component and 5 bits for the blue color component. *The working projector on the right and its real projection on the left. An OnyxOS guest program writes the 640×480 framebuffer. (Minecraft 26.1.2)* Projectors need to be powered directly to function. The device bus cannot provide enough energy on its own. When insufficiently powered, this is indicated by a red glow in the projector's lens. On a Linux system, projectors will typically appear as */dev/fbX* devices. To send data to the framebuffer, it is possible to write to these devices. For example, to clear a framebuffer one might pipe zeros to the device like so: *cat /dev/zero > /dev/fb0*. When using the default Linux distribution, the [keyboard](/en/block/keyboard) may be used, to send input to the virtual terminal, running on the first connected framebuffer. Computers *have to be shut down* before installing or removing this component. Installing it while the computer is running will have no effect, removing it may lead to system errors. ## Crafting recipes - [Projector](/en/recipes#recipe-projector) --- [OC2R source](https://github.com/DivByDiamond/OC2R/blob/39eb8109e2e38fdb047af98d8e6f7ded0194f498/src/main/resources/assets/oc2r/doc/en_us/block/projector.md) · `39eb8109e2e3`

pages.title: Redstone Interface
pages.body:
# Redstone Interface
`oc2r:redstone_interface`

The redstone interface provides an omnidirectional bus to receive and emit redstone signals.

Use this to interact with primitive devices, such as doors and lamps, or other machinery offering a redstone based protocol.

This is a high level device. It must be controlled using the high level device API. The default Linux distribution offers Lua libraries for this API. For example:  
*local d = require("devices")*  
*local r = d:find("redstone")*  
*r:setRedstoneOutput("up", 15)*

## API
Device name: *redstone*

### Sides
The side parameter in the following methods represents a side local to the device block. Valid values are: *up*, *down*, *left*, *right*, *front*, *back*, *north*, *south*, *west* and *east*.

Each face of the block has an indicator for convenience. Side names represent the names with the block seen from the primary face (indicated by a single marking). When looking at the primary face:
- *front* and *south* is the face we are looking at.
- *back* and *north* is the face behind the block.
- *left* and *west* is the face to our left.
- *right* and *east* is the face to our right.
- *up* and *down* are the top and bottom faces.

### Methods
*getRedstoneInput(side):number* gets the received redstone signal for the specified side.
- *side* is a string representing the side to get the input on. See the "Sides" section.
- Returns the number representing the current input signal strength.

*setRedstoneOutput(side, value:number)* sets the emitted redstone signal for the specified side.
- *side* is a string representing the side to set the signal on. See the "Sides" section.
- *value* is a number representing the signal strength to set in the range of [0, 15].

*getRedstoneOutput(side):number* gets the emitted redstone signal for the specified side.
- *side* is a string representing the side to get the output on. See the "Sides" section.
- Returns the number representing the current output signal strength.

<!-- wiki-recipes -->
## Crafting recipes

- [Redstone Interface](/en/recipes#recipe-redstone_interface)
<!-- /wiki-recipes -->

pages.body:
# Speaker
`oc2r:speaker`

Connect the speaker through a bus interface and cable. Its RPC device name is *speaker*. Example: *local s = require("devices"):find("speaker")*, then *s:beep(880, 500)*.

*beep(frequency,duration)* and its alias *playTone* accept 20–20000 Hz and 20–5000 milliseconds. *write(data)* accepts numeric byte arrays containing 44100 Hz, mono, signed 16-bit little-endian PCM. See the [sound card](/en/item/sound_card) for the PCM format and RPC throughput limitations.

The speaker does not offer the sound card's *playSound* or *findSound* methods.

# VXLAN hub
`oc2r:vxlan_hub`

Bridges an in-game Ethernet network to an external VXLAN tunnel over UDP. Connect it to network devices rather than the device bus. External connectivity requires the server administrator to enable and configure the common config vxlan section. Local forwarding acts as a hub. It is separate from paired tunnel cards and GPS radio networks.

pages.title: Getting Started
pages.body: # Getting Started Start with a [computer](/en/block/computer), one [CPU](/en/item/cpu), and four 8 MiB [memory](/en/item/memory) modules (32 MiB total is a practical starting configuration). The survival computer recipe includes a Linux [firmware chip](/en/item/flash_memory); a plain computer obtained in another way may need that chip installed separately. Place the computer and use a [scrench](/en/item/wrench) to open its inventory. Install the CPU, RAM and firmware in their dedicated slots. The preconfigured creative computer already contains components. Supply energy and check the energy bar's tooltip for stored energy and consumption. Then open the terminal and press its power button. Wait for the login prompt and log in as *root*. The bundled Linux boots from a built-in writable root filesystem. An extra hard drive and the old wrench-prepared "Linux disk" are not required. Extra [hard drives](/en/item/hard_drive) are data disks; formatting them erases their contents. The firmware loads the kernel from the built-in root disk. The computer's own terminal works without a GPU. For a [monitor](/en/block/monitor), install a [GPU](/en/item/gpu), connect the monitor through [bus interfaces](/en/block/bus_interface) and [cables](/en/block/bus_cable), and power the display. A [projector](/en/block/projector) is a separate fixed-resolution framebuffer device. Shut down before replacing native components. If boot fails, check CPU, RAM, firmware, energy and the error shown in the terminal. Changing the server's component/energy settings can change the required setup. See [basics](/en/basics), [scripting](/en/scripting), [networking](/en/networking) and [robotics](/en/robotics) for the next steps. ## In game Actual Minecraft 26.1.2 screenshots from the OC2R demonstration world. *A Linux terminal excerpt showing kernel 6.6.32 and Lua 5.4.6 inside the OC2R guest. (Minecraft 26.1.2)* --- [OC2R source](https://github.com/DivByDiamond/OC2R/blob/39eb8109e2e38fdb047af98d8e6f7ded0194f498/src/main/resources/assets/oc2r/doc/en_us/getting_started.md) · `39eb8109e2e3`

pages.title: Block Operations Module
pages.body:
# Block Operations Module
`oc2r:block_operations_module`

The block operations module provides to [robots](/en/item/robot) the ability to break and place blocks in the world.

## API
Device name: *block_operations*

This is a high level API device. It can be controlled using Lua in the default Linux distribution. For example:  
*local d = require("devices")*  
*local m = d:find("block_operations")*  
*m:excavate("front")*

### Sides
The side parameter in the following methods represents a direction from the perspective of the robot. Valid values are: *front*, *up* and *down*.

### Methods
*excavate([side]):boolean* tries to break a block in the specified direction. Collected blocks will be inserted starting at the currently selected inventory slot. If the selected slot is full, the next slot will be used, and so on. If the inventory has no space for the dropped block, it will drop into the world.
- *side* is the relative direction in to break a block in. Optional, defaults to *front*. See the "Sides" section.
- Returns whether the operation was successful.

*place([side]):boolean* tries to place a block in the specified direction. Blocks will be placed from the currently selected inventory slot. If the slot is empty, no block will be placed.
- *side* is the relative direction to place the block in. Optional, defaults to *front*. See the "Sides" section.
- Returns whether the operation was successful.

*durability():number* returns the remaining durability of the module's excavation tool. Once the durability has reached zero, no further excavation operations can be performed until it is repaired.
- Returns the remaining durability of the module's excavation tool

*repair():boolean* attempts to repair the module's excavation tool using materials in the currently selected inventory slot. This method will consume one item at a time. Any regular tool may act as the source for repair materials, such as pickaxes and shovels. The quality of the tool directly effects the amount of durability restored.
- Returns whether some material could be used to repair the module's excavation tool.

<!-- wiki-recipes -->
## Crafting recipes

- [Block Operations Module](/en/recipes#recipe-block_operations_module)
<!-- /wiki-recipes -->

pages.body:
# CPU
`oc2r:cpu_tier_1`

A CPU is required to start a computer or robot. Install one in its CPU slot while the machine is off. The implemented guest architecture is single-core 64-bit RISC-V with floating-point support. Lua is a guest program, not a separate processor architecture.

The four normal tiers default to 50, 100, 200 and 400 MHz. Frequency is assigned when the item is registered; its displayed name reports the assigned value. The server configuration defines tier settings. The creative processor has a separate 1 GHz setting. Emulated frequency is a target and does not guarantee host performance.

A faster CPU does not replace [RAM](/en/item/memory), firmware or energy. See [getting started](/en/getting_started).

# Crafting Module
`oc2r:crafting_module`

The crafting module provides to [robots](/en/item/robot) the ability to craft items from a crafting grid.

## API
Device name: *crafting*

This is a high level API device. It can be controlled using Lua in the default Linux distribution. For example:  
*local d = require("devices")*  
*local c = d:find("crafting")*  
*c:craft()*

The top part of the robot's inventory, slots *0* to *8*, serves as the crafting grid. Crafted items go into the bottom row, starting at the selected slot.

### Methods
*craft():number* tries to craft once from the crafting grid. Fails if the grid matches no recipe or the result does not fit into the bottom row.
- Returns the number of items crafted, or *0* if crafting failed.

pages.title: File Import/Export Card
pages.body:
# File Import/Export Card
`oc2r:file_import_export_card`

This RPC device, named *file_import_export*, transfers files between the guest and players currently using its terminal. Upload uses the first responding player; downloads are offered to all current terminal users. With no users present, an import request returns false.

The old *import.lua* and *export.lua* helpers are not bundled in the current package. Use the device API from a guest program, or provide your own wrappers. See [scripting](/en/scripting) for Lua setup and discovery.

## API

*beginExportFile(name)* starts an export; *writeExportFile(data)* appends numeric byte arrays; *finishExportFile()* opens the players' save dialogs. The export limit is 1048575 bytes.

*requestImportFile():boolean* opens an upload dialog. Poll *beginImportFile()* until it returns file metadata (*name*, *size*), then call *readImportFile()* for numeric byte chunks until an empty array marks the end. Cancellation raises an error. Calls must follow this order; overlapping transfers are rejected.

<!-- wiki-recipes -->
## Crafting recipes

- [File Import/Export Card](/en/recipes#recipe-file_import_export_card)
<!-- /wiki-recipes -->

pages.title: Flash Memory
pages.body:
# Flash Memory
`oc2r:flash_memory`

A flash chip contains the initial code executed by the [computer](/en/block/computer) or [robot](/en/item/robot). Blank chips and chips with bundled firmware are different items. A blank chip alone does not provide a working OS.

The bundled Linux firmware is a small boot ROM; it loads the kernel from the built-in root disk. The kernel is no longer embedded in this firmware, and an additional hard drive is not required for the default Linux boot.

To obtain bundled firmware through crafting, combine the largest blank flash chip with a [scrench](/en/item/wrench) for Linux; combine the resulting Linux chip with a scrench again for OnyxOS firmware. The tool is returned. Do not confuse a firmware recipe with the recipe that clears a chip.

The [flash memory flasher](/en/block/media_station) also accepts bundled firmware and local images through its interface. Shut down before replacing a computer's firmware. Custom firmware must match the emulated hardware and provide its own boot requirements.

pages.title: GPU
pages.body: # GPU `oc2r:gpu_tier_1` Install a GPU in a computer's GPU slot before booting to enable its connected [monitors](/en/block/monitor). Without a GPU, a monitor has no framebuffer device and stays dark. The computer's own text terminal still works. *Two separate monitors attached to one computer show independent framebuffers at the same time: telemetry and the ONYX OS display. (Minecraft 26.1.2)* The four GPU tiers provide 320 by 200, 640 by 400, 1024 by 768 and 1920 by 1080 pixels. A monitor uses the installed GPU's resolution, not a fixed 640 by 480 image. Larger images require more resources and bandwidth. The [projector](/en/block/projector) is a separate 640 by 480 device. Shut down before changing the GPU. The display still needs a bus connection and energy; a GPU alone does not power it. ## Crafting recipes - [GPU Tier 1](/en/recipes#recipe-gpu_tier_1) - [GPU Tier 2](/en/recipes#recipe-gpu_tier_2) - [GPU Tier 3](/en/recipes#recipe-gpu_tier_3) - [GPU Tier 4](/en/recipes#recipe-gpu_tier_4) --- [OC2R source](https://github.com/DivByDiamond/OC2R/blob/39eb8109e2e38fdb047af98d8e6f7ded0194f498/src/main/resources/assets/oc2r/doc/en_us/item/gpu.md) · `39eb8109e2e3`

pages.title: Hard Drive
pages.body:
# Hard Drive
`oc2r:hard_drive_large`

Hard drives add persistent storage to [computers](/en/block/computer) and [robots](/en/item/robot). The default Linux already has a built-in writable root disk: an extra hard drive is optional. Its overlay is saved with the VM, independently of removable disks.

Extra disks appear as Linux block devices such as */dev/vdb*. Device letters depend on the attached devices: inspect */proc/partitions* before formatting. Format a new data disk, create a mount directory and mount it using the tools described for the [disk drive](/en/block/media_station). Formatting destroys existing data. Never format the built-in root disk to prepare an extra data disk.

The OnyxOS disk recipe uses the medium hard drive; it is separate from the standard Linux boot path. Custom OS images can require a different disk layout.

Shut down before installing or removing a hard drive. Preserve the original item to preserve its data.

<!-- wiki-recipes -->

pages.title: Internet Card
pages.body:
# Internet Card
`oc2r:internet_card`

This native device provides an Ethernet connection through the real Minecraft server's Internet adapter. Internet access is disabled by default and requires administrator configuration. Host restrictions and session limits apply.

Unlike a cable LAN, this is a point-to-point link without a DHCP server. Configure the guest's interface with a static address and suitable route; the adapter answers ARP. *setup-network.lua* is not included. Actual allowed destinations depend on the server's *deniedHosts* configuration. An ordinary NIC and local cables do not grant Internet access on their own.

Shut down before installing or removing this card. The [Internet gateway](/en/block/internet_gateway) can expose a host-backed connection to a cable network instead.

pages.title: Inventory Operations Module
pages.body:
# Inventory Operations Module
`oc2r:inventory_operations_module`

The inventory operations module provides to [robots](/en/item/robot) the ability to insert and extract items from inventories in the world. This supports both block and entity inventories.

## API
Device name: *inventory_operations*

This is a high level API device. It can be controlled using Lua in the default Linux distribution. For example:  
*local d = require("devices")*  
*local m = d:find("inventory_operations")*  
*m:drop(1, "front")*

### Sides
The side parameter in the following methods represents a direction from the perspective of the robot. Valid values are: *front*, *up* and *down*.

### Methods
*move(fromSlot:number,intoSlot:number,count:number)* tries to move the specified number of items from one robot inventory slot to another.
- *fromSlot* is the slot to extract items from.
- *intoSlot* is the slot to insert items into.
- *count* is the number of items to move.

*drop(count:number[,side]):number* tries to drop items from the specified slot in the specified direction. It will drop items either into an inventory, or the world if no inventory is present.
- *count* is the number of items to drop.
- *side* is the relative direction to drop the items in. Optional, defaults to *front*. See the "Sides" section.
- Returns the number of items dropped.

*dropInto(intoSlot:number,count:number[,side]):number* tries to drop items from the specified slot into the specified slot of an inventory in the specified direction. It will only drop items into an inventory.
- *intoSlot* is the slot to insert the items into.
- *count* is the number of items to drop.
- *side* is the relative direction to drop the items in. Optional, defaults to *front*. See the "Sides" section.
- Returns the number of items dropped.

*take(count:number[,side]):number* tries to take the specified number of items from the specified direction. It will take items from either an inventory, or the world if no inventory is present.
- *count* is the number of items to take.
- *side* is the relative direction to take the items from. Optional, defaults to *front*. See the "Sides" section.
- Returns the number of items taken.

*takeFrom(fromSlot:number,count:number[,side]):number* tries to take the specified number of items from the specified slot from an inventory in the specified direction. It will only take items from an inventory.
- *fromSlot* is the slot to take the items from.
- *count* is the number of items to take.
- *side* is the relative direction to take the items from. Optional, defaults to *front*. See the "Sides" section.
- Returns the number of items taken.

<!-- wiki-recipes -->
## Crafting recipes

- [Inventory Operations Module](/en/recipes#recipe-inventory_operations_module)
<!-- /wiki-recipes -->

# Memory
`oc2r:memory_large`

The random access memory (RAM) device provides working memory to [computers](/en/block/computer) and [robots](/en/item/robot).

As opposed to [hard drives](/en/item/hard_drive), this memory is volatile and will be cleared when a computer powers down. RAM is required by the bundled firmware and Linux. Modules provide 2, 4, 8 or 16 MiB each.

Also see the [getting started](/en/getting_started) manual entry.

Computers *have to be shut down* before installing or removing this component. Installing it while the computer is running will have no effect, removing it may lead to system errors.

`oc2r:network_interface_card`

The network interface card (NIC) allows [computers](/en/block/computer) to send messages to and receive messages from [network connectors](/en/block/network_connector) attached to the computer.

# Redstone Interface Card
`oc2r:redstone_interface_card`

The redstone interface card is a more compact version of the [redstone interface block](/en/block/redstone_interface). It enables users to build more compact designs.

The API of this device is identical to that of the redstone interface block.

pages.title: Robot
pages.body: # Robot `oc2r:robot` Robots are essentially mobile [computers](/en/block/computer). Due to their non-stationary nature, there is some behavior that differs from regular computers. They cannot connect to [bus interfaces](/en/block/bus_interface). Instead of card devices, they support module devices. These are specialized devices taking into account the robots' mobility. *The demonstration robot on its charger, with a chest above it. (Minecraft 26.1.2)* Robots have a fixed-size inventory and sport a state-of-the-art energy storage. Only the regular inventory of robots can be automatically filled and emptied, for example by devices such as a hopper. The component inventory of the robot must be manually configured. In their default configuration, robots cannot interact with their own inventory. Use an [inventory operations module](/en/item/inventory_operations_module) to enable robots to move items in their own inventory, as well as to insert and extract items to and from other inventories. To recharge a robot, it is recommended to make use the [charger](/en/block/charger). It is possible for robots to recharge themselves by simply moving on top of a charger. Alternatively, they may be placed into an inventory on top of the charger. The default Linux distribution provides a utility Lua library, *robot*, that eases controlling robots. The underlying API offers asynchronous methods for movement. The library implements synchronous alternatives, making sequential programming more convenient. ## API Device name: *robot* This is a high level API device. It can be controlled using Lua in the default Linux distribution. For example: *local d = require("devices")* *local r = d:find("robot")* *r:move("forward")* ### Directions The direction parameter in the following methods represents a direction relative to the robot. Valid values are: *forward*, *backward*, *upward*, *downward* for movement actions, *left* and *right* for rotation actions. These directions are always from the point of view of the robot at the time it executes an action. Short form aliases of these values can be used for convenience: *back*, *up*, *down*. For extreme brevity, the initial letter of each direction can be used as well. ### Methods These methods are available on the underlying robot device. Note that the library offers useful wrapper for all of these. It is recommended to use the library instead of interacting with the device directly. *getEnergyStored():number* returns the current amount of energy stored in the robot's internal energy storage. - Returns the stored amount of energy. *getEnergyCapacity():number* returns the maximum amount of energy that can be stored in the robot's internal energy storage. - Returns the maximum amount of energy stored. *getSelectedSlot():number* returns the currently selected robot inventory slot. This is used by many modules as an implicit input. - Returns the index of the selected inventory slot. *setSelectedSlot(slot:number)* sets the currently selected robot inventory slot. This is used by many modules as an implicit input. - *slot* is the index of the inventory slot to select. *getStackInSlot(slot:number):table* gets a description of the item in the specified slot. - *slot* is the index of the slot to get the item description for. *move(direction):boolean* tries to enqueue a movement action in the specified direction. - *direction* is the direction to move in. - Returns whether the action was enqueued successfully. *turn(direction):boolean* tries to enqueue a turn action towards the specified direction. - *direction* is the direction to turn towards. - Returns whether the action was enqueued successfully. *getLastActionId():number* returns the opaque id of the last enqueued action. Call this after a successful *move()* or *turn()* call to obtain the id associated with the enqueued action. - Returns the id of the last enqueued action. *getQueuedActionCount():number* returns the number of actions currently waiting in the action queue to be processed. Use this to wait for actions to finish when enqueueing fails. - Returns the number of currently pending actions. *getActionResult(actionId:number):string* returns the result of the action with the specified id. Action ids can be obtained from *getLastActionId()*. Only a limited number of past action results are available. - Returns the result for the specified action id, or nothing if unavailable. When available, possible values are: *INCOMPLETE*, *SUCCESS* and *FAILURE*. *getFacing():string* returns the compass direction the robot is facing: *north*, *south*, *east* or *west*. - Returns the facing direction name. *getPosition():table* returns the body position relative to the localization origin, as a table with *x* (east), *y* (up) and *z* (south) fields. The origin is set when the robot is first placed and recalibrated with *calibratePosition()*; crossing into another dimension resets it. - Returns the relative position table. *calibratePosition()* resets the localization origin to the robot's current body position, so *getPosition()* reads *(0, 0, 0)* again. ### Library API - Library name: *robot* This is a Lua library. It can be used in the default Linux distribution. For example: *local r = require("robot")* *r.move("forward")* *r.turn("left")* ### Methods *energy():number* returns the current amount of energy stored in the robot's internal energy storage. - Returns the stored amount of energy. *capacity():number* returns the maximum amount of energy that can be stored in the robot's internal energy storage. - Returns the maximum amount of energy stored. *slot():number* returns the currently selected robot inventory slot. This is used by many modules as an implicit input. - Returns the index of the selected inventory slot. *slot(slot:number):number* sets the currently selected robot inventory slot. This is used by many modules as an implicit input. - *slot* is the index of the inventory slot to select. - Returns the index of the newly selected slot. This may differ from *slot* if the specified value was invalid. *stack([slot:number]):table* gets a description of the item in the specified slot. - *slot* is the index of the slot to get the item description for. Optional, defaults to *slot()*. *move(direction):boolean* tries to move into the specified direction. Blocks until the movement operation has completed. - *direction* is the direction to move in. - Returns whether the operation was successful. *moveAsync(direction)* tries to asynchronously move into the specified direction. Blocks until the action was successfully enqueued. - *direction* is the direction to move in. *turn(direction):boolean* tries to turn towards the specified direction. Blocks until the rotation operation has completed. - *direction* is the direction to turn towards. - Returns whether the operation was successfully. *turnAsync(direction)* tries to asynchronously turn into the specified direction. Blocks until the action was successfully enqueued. - *direction* is the direction to turn towards. Inventory indices start at zero. The direct *setSelectedSlot* call returns no value; read *getSelectedSlot()* afterwards. The Lua *robot.slot(value)* wrapper returns the resulting selected slot. The Lua library also provides *facing()*, *position()* and *calibrate()* as wrappers for the corresponding device methods. ## Crafting recipes - [Robot](/en/recipes#recipe-robot) --- [OC2R source](https://github.com/DivByDiamond/OC2R/blob/39eb8109e2e38fdb047af98d8e6f7ded0194f498/src/main/resources/assets/oc2r/doc/en_us/item/robot.md) · `39eb8109e2e3`

pages.title: Scanner Module
pages.body:
# Scanner Module
`oc2r:scanner_module`

The scanner module provides to [robots](/en/item/robot) the ability to inspect the block, fluid and entities on one of its sides, to measure the hardness of the blocks around it, and to check whether it can see the sky.

## API
Device name: *scanner*

This is a high level API device. It can be controlled using Lua in the default Linux distribution. For example:  
*local d = require("devices")*  
*local s = d:find("scanner")*  
*s:scan()*

### Sides
The side parameter of *inspect()* represents a face of the robot. Valid values are: *front*, *up* and *down*.

### Scanning
*scan()* measures the hardness of every block in a cube of seven by seven by seven blocks with the robot at its center. Positions use the axes of the robot's *getPosition()*: *x* grows towards east, *y* upward and *z* towards south.

The RPC result is a Lua table of 343 unsigned numbers (0 to 255), one per block, not a string. Blocks are ordered by *y*, then *z*, then *x*, each from *-3* to *3*, so the result is a stack of horizontal layers from bottom to top, and *x* changes fastest. The block at offset *x*, *y*, *z* from the robot is at index `(y + 3) * 7 * 7 + (z + 3) * 7 + (x + 3)`, counting from zero. Since Lua counts from one, this is equivalent to *hardness[index + 1]*.

Each byte encodes air as *0*, any fluid as *254* and unbreakable or unscannable blocks as *255*. Regular blocks are encoded as hardness mapped into the *1* to *253* range.

After a scan, the scanner needs five seconds to recharge. Scanning while it recharges fails.

### Fluids
Fluids are always reported by their source fluid, such as *minecraft:water*.

### Entities
Entities are reported by identifier, such as *minecraft:sheep*, closest first. At most twenty are listed.

### Methods
*inspect(side):table* identifies the block, fluid and entities in the space on the specified side of the robot.
- *side* is the side to look at: *front*, *up* or *down*.
- Returns a table with the *block* and *fluid*, if present, and a list of *entities*.

*scan():table* measures the hardness of the blocks around the robot and lists nearby entities.
- Returns a table with the block *hardness* as a numeric array, see above, and the list of *entities* in the scanned cube.

*canSeeSky():boolean* checks whether the robot's space gets full sky light.
- Returns whether the sky is visible.

*getScanLayer(layer:number):table* reads one layer of the last scan. Fails if there was no scan yet.
- *layer* is the layer, 0 to 6 from bottom to top.
- Returns a table of 49 numbers, the hardness of each block in the layer.

<!-- wiki-recipes -->
## Crafting recipes

- [Scanner Module](/en/recipes#recipe-scanner_module)
<!-- /wiki-recipes -->

pages.title: Sound Card
pages.body:
# Sound Card
`oc2r:sound_card`

The sound card enables playing back various sound effects from its vast library of life-like samples. Due to internal engineering constraints, playback of sequential effects requires a small pause. Attempts to play back additional effects in this time window will have no effect.

This is a high level device. It must be controlled using the high level device API. The default Linux distribution offers Lua libraries for this API. For example:  
*local d = require("devices")*  
*local s = d:find("sound")*  
*s:playSound("entity.creeper.primed")*

## API
Device name: *sound*

### Methods
*playSound(name:string[,volume:float,pitch:float])* plays back the sound effect with the specified name.
- *name* is the name of the effect to play.
- *volume* is the volume at which to play the effect in the range from *0* to *1*, with *1* being the normal volume. Optional, defaulting to *1*.
- *pitch* is the pitch at which to play the effect in the range from *0.5* to *2*, with *1* being the normal pitch. Optional, defaulting to *1*.
- Throws if the specified name is invalid.

*findSound(name:string):table* returns a list of available sound effects matching the given name. Note that the number of results is limited, so overly generic queries will result in truncated results.
- *name* the name query to search for.
- Returns a list of sound effect names matching the query string.

## Tone and PCM

*beep(frequency:number,duration:number)* plays a tone from 20 to 20000 Hz for 20 to 5000 milliseconds. *playTone* is an alias. Example: *s:beep(880, 500)*.

*write(data:table)* accepts a numeric byte array of signed 16-bit little-endian mono PCM at 44100 Hz. Each sample occupies two bytes. RPC uses JSON arrays, not Lua binary strings. Send small chunks and pace them; the card enforces a configurable byte budget (131072 bytes/second by default). RPC throughput can be much lower than real-time audio. This is not an MP3/WAV decoder; remove container headers and supply decoded PCM.

*findSound* returns at most 25 matching names. The effect cooldown applies to *playSound*. For an external bus device with tone/PCM support, see the [speaker](/en/block/speaker).

<!-- wiki-recipes -->
## Crafting recipes

- [Sound Card](/en/recipes#recipe-sound_card)
<!-- /wiki-recipes -->

# Scrench
`oc2r:wrench`

The wrench-screwdriver multi-tool, nicknamed "Scrench", can be used to directly access the configuration of some blocks, such as [computers](/en/block/computer).

It is required to configure some devices such as [bus interfaces](/en/block/bus_interface). It may also be used to quickly dismantle some devices, such as [cables](/en/block/bus_cable).

This tool can also be used to remove facades from cables.

pages.title: Networking
pages.body: # Networking Connect [network connectors](/en/block/network_connector) with [network cables](/en/item/network_cable), and install a [network interface card](/en/item/network_interface_card) in each computer. Connectors attach to the computer's non-front faces. The card's configuration enables or disables its individual sides. *Two OnyxOS computers connected by a blue network cable. This local TCP example does not use the Internet. (Minecraft 26.1.2)* Connectors relay frames between cable links. Use a [hub](/en/block/network_hub) for branches. Avoid loops: forwarded frames consume a finite hop budget, but cycles can still create duplicates before that budget expires. ## Linux setup Shut down before installing a network card, then boot Linux. Discover the interface in the shell: ```sh ifconfig -a ``` For a two-computer LAN, run this on the first computer, replacing `eth0` if needed: ```sh ifconfig eth0 192.168.50.1 netmask 255.255.255.0 up ``` On the second computer: ```sh ifconfig eth0 192.168.50.2 netmask 255.255.255.0 up ``` Test from the first computer: ```sh ping 192.168.50.2 ``` These are temporary settings; persistent setup uses the guest's Linux network configuration. The old *setup-network.lua* wizard is not included in the current bundled scripts. There is no automatic DHCP server in a cable or hub. A DHCP client such as *udhcpc -i eth0* requires an actual DHCP server on that network. Do not run multiple DHCP servers or overlap the dynamic pool with static addresses. The guest includes *ssh* and *scp* clients. Remote login also needs a running SSH server on the destination. LuaSocket is available for custom guest networking. An [Internet card](/en/item/internet_card) uses a separate host-backed point-to-point connection; it is not configured like a DHCP cable LAN. ## In game Actual Minecraft 26.1.2 screenshots from the OC2R demonstration world. *A terminal excerpt: the client received ONYX-TCP-ECHO from the second computer over the local network. (Minecraft 26.1.2)* --- [OC2R source](https://github.com/DivByDiamond/OC2R/blob/39eb8109e2e38fdb047af98d8e6f7ded0194f498/src/main/resources/assets/oc2r/doc/en_us/networking.md) · `39eb8109e2e3`

pages.body:
# Minecraft versions and loaders

The current OC2R source has six build targets. Choose an artifact matching both your Minecraft version and loader.

## Implemented targets

| Minecraft | NeoForge | Fabric | Java |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1.21.1 | Implemented | Implemented | 21 |
| 26.1.2 | Implemented | Implemented | 25 |
| 26.2 | Implemented | Implemented | 25 |

Fabric 26.1.2 and 26.2 have been accepted, merged and verified in CI. The earlier statement that Fabric 26.x was future work is outdated. Local acceptance included server tests and client runs on both modern versions.

## Download availability

Check the artifacts in [OC2R releases](https://github.com/DivByDiamond/OC2R/releases). An implemented build target does not establish publication on every distribution platform. In the source revision linked below, publication of the new Fabric 26.x targets is a separate step deferred at the owner's request.

NeoForge and Fabric artifacts are not interchangeable. Install Fabric API separately. Team Reborn Energy and Forge Config API Port are bundled in the OC2R artifacts, with compatible versions selected by the mod build.

## Reading the acceptance reports

Dated roadmap sections preserve earlier limitations. The current summary records all six targets as implemented. Use the current acceptance report for implementation status and the release page for downloadable artifacts.

The [Fabric 26.x acceptance report](https://github.com/DivByDiamond/OC2R/blob/39eb8109e2e38fdb047af98d8e6f7ded0194f498/docs/roadmap/fabric-26-acceptance.md) contains the target matrix and validation results. Server settings may change hardware characteristics.

pages.title: Cable System Rework — Design (Core)
pages.body:
# Cable System Rework — Design (Core)

Design doc for replacing OC2R's two independent, ad-hoc wiring mechanisms
with one unified cable system. Written 2026-09-15, not yet implemented —
this is the plan, not the build. Sub-projects after this one (wrench
tool/UX, cross-mod tool-tag compatibility, migrating existing player
builds) get their own specs when work starts on them.

## Why

Today there are **two unrelated block types** doing "wire two things
together", and their bugs are actually the same bug wearing two faces:

- **`BusCableBlockEntity`/`DeviceBusElement`** (device bus: CPU↔memory↔
  disk↔monitor↔keyboard) — full graph BFS re-scan (`BusElementManager.
  collectBusElements`) on *every* topology change, hard-capped at 128
  elements (`TOO_COMPLEX`), and a `MULTIPLE_CONTROLLERS` state that
  freezes the whole bus for 5s if two computers land on one segment.
- **`NetworkConnectorBlockEntity`** (internet mesh / energy) — a
  completely separate point-to-point model: max 2 connections per
  connector, 16-block max distance, raycast-obstruction check, manual
  "owned cable" bookkeeping for who respawns the item on disconnect.

Reported symptoms — cables appearing out of nowhere, energy silently
stopping over distance, lag on runs with turns, breaking/replacing a
cable leaving stale connections, energy and device-bus traffic
conflicting on the same run — all trace back to the same root cause:
**cached neighbor/network state that isn't strictly derived from one
source of truth, and gets re-derived inconsistently between client and
server or after a chunk reload.** Two more targeted rescans and one more
special-case flag do not fix that; removing the mutable cached state
does.

## Scope of this document

One unified cable block replacing both `BusCable` and `NetworkConnector`.
Carries device-bus traffic, energy, and internet-mesh traffic over the
same physical run — the player places one kind of wire, not two.

Out of scope for this doc (own future specs):
- The wrench/tool UX for per-face disconnect (needs this core to exist
  first).
- Migrating existing player worlds off `BusCable`/`NetworkConnector`.
- Any device-sharing feature beyond the ownership model below (e.g. an
  explicitly "shareable" monitor).

## Connection model

**Auto-connect by adjacency.** Two cable blocks that are face-adjacent
are connected — no player action. A cable adjacent to a device (computer,
monitor, energy-consuming block, etc.) auto-connects if that device's
face offers a compatible capability, same as the current per-face
NeoForge capability lookup already used by `AbstractBlockDeviceBusElement
.getNeighbors()`.

**Per-face override, in the data model from day one.** Each cable BE
stores a per-face connection state — `AUTO` (default) / `FORCED_ON` /
`FORCED_OFF` — even before the wrench tool that lets a player set it
exists. Baking this into the save format now avoids a data migration
later when the wrench sub-project ships.

**`NetworkConnectorBlockEntity` is deliberately removed, not folded in.**
Its whole reason to exist — a through-air link up to 16 blocks with an
obstruction check, no physical cable required — has no equivalent in an
adjacency-based model *by definition*. This is an intentional feature
loss, written down here so it doesn't surface later as "wait, where did
long-distance connectors go?" A pair of wireless endpoint blocks
replicating that use case is a plausible future sub-project, not part of
this core rework.

**Hub and switch blocks are removed too.** Internet-mesh topology becomes
simply "which cable network is this computer's card connected to" — the
whole connected network already behaves like one big switch, so
`NetworkHubBlockEntity`/`NetworkSwitchBlockEntity`'s job is subsumed by
the cable network itself.

## Topology: no persistent network objects

**The most consequential decision in this design, so stated plainly:**
there is no network object saved to NBT, no network ID, no merge/split
bookkeeping surviving a save. This directly targets the "phantom
cable"/"broke on reload" bug class — the entire point-of-failure that
persistent, incrementally-merged network state represents (an old,
well-documented pain point in this genre of mod — Mekanism/AE2 grid code
has years of exactly this class of desync bug) is designed out by not
having that state exist at all.

Instead:
- Each cable BE holds a **cache reference** to "the network this cable
  currently belongs to" — purely in memory, never serialized.
- Any topology-relevant event invalidates that cache: block placed,
  block broken/removed, `onLoad`/chunk load-unload, a wrench toggling a
  per-face override.
- On the next access after invalidation, a **fresh BFS runs from the
  requesting cable**, walking currently-loaded neighbors, and the result
  (the resolved network view) is written back into every visited BE's
  cache.
- After a server restart, or a chunk reload, the network is silently
  rebuilt lazily on first access — there is nothing to "recover" because
  nothing persisted that could go stale.

**Performance framing**: this is not a regression from removing the 128
cap's motivation. The old system's cost was never the BFS itself — it
was re-running that BFS (and re-registering every capability listener)
from `serverTick()` on a schedule, whether or not anything changed.
Removing all topology work from `tick()` (see below) means a full BFS
becomes an O(N) cost paid **once per player action** (place, break,
wrench), not a recurring per-tick cost — a full rebuild of a large
network is milliseconds, and it simply doesn't happen unless something
actually changed.

**The 128-element hard cap is replaced by a generous, configurable
default (start at ~1024)**, and exceeding it no longer freezes the whole
network. The player-facing effect changes from "the entire bus goes
`TOO_COMPLEX` and stops" to "the single device that pushed the network
over the limit is flagged unavailable, everything else keeps working" —
consistent with the UX principle that one bad connection must not take
down a working network.

**Zero topology work happens in `tick()`.** The only thing that ticks is
energy distribution across an already-resolved network view (see below).
Topology is entirely event-driven.

## Device ownership

Multiple computers can legally share one physical network segment now
(no more `MULTIPLE_CONTROLLERS` error state) — the wiring merges without
friction. But device *ownership* stays exclusive: a hard drive mounted
by two independent guest kernels with no coordination is filesystem
corruption, not a shared resource, so "just let both computers use it"
is not on the table for storage/CPU/memory-class devices.

**Ownership is computed, never stored.** On each network rebuild, every
device's owning controller is derived deterministically from the
currently-*loaded* set of controllers on that network — e.g. the
controller at the lowest `BlockPos`. No ownership record is saved
anywhere, so there is nothing to desync. A practical side effect: if the
owning computer's chunk unloads, ownership deterministically re-derives
to the next controller on the next rebuild — failover happens for free,
with no special-cased "handle owner disappearing" logic.

**Ownership is visible, never silent.** A controller that loses the race
for a device does not just fail to see it — it sees the device listed
as **occupied, naming the owning computer**, both through the API (so
guest-side tooling can report it) and via an in-world tooltip on the
device block. A player who builds a second computer onto an existing
segment and finds their disk missing gets an explicit reason, not silent
unavailability they have to debug by breaking cables at random.

## Energy

**No network-level energy buffer.** Each cable BE holds its own small
energy buffer, saved with that block entity like any other stateful
block — never centralized in the (unsaved, lazily-rebuilt) network
object, which would have nowhere durable to put the energy when a chunk
unloads mid-transfer. The network is purely a *view* that aggregates and
routes between per-cable buffers; it owns no state of its own.

**External faces expose a receive-only `IEnergyStorage`** (`canExtract()`
returns `false`). This is what makes "accept energy from other mods'
cables" (Mekanism Universal Cable, Pipez Energy Pipe, anything using the
standard capability) close to free — no custom bridge, just implementing
the capability every energy-producing mod already knows how to push
into. Explicitly one-directional: OC2R's network draws power from
adjacent foreign networks, it does not export into them.

## Traffic separation

One cable block, three logically separate "lanes" riding the same
resolved network view — invisible to the player, no default-on
configuration surface:

1. **Device-bus** — RPC/VM-device traffic (CPU, memory, disk, monitor,
   keyboard), subject to the ownership model above.
2. **Energy** — per-cable buffers, receive-only foreign-capability faces,
   ticked distribution.
3. **Internet-mesh** — replaces hub/switch; membership in the network is
   membership in the mesh.

Splitting these was the direct fix for the "energy transfer blocks data
transfer on the same run" symptom: today they collide because the mental
model of "one wire" doesn't match the physical model of "two different
block types, only one of which even carries device-bus traffic." Making
one block type carry all three lanes, cleanly separated internally,
closes that gap.

## UX principles (requirements, not suggestions)

1. **Nothing happens silently.** A connection forming/breaking is
   visible (cable model updates per-face); a wrench interaction gives
   immediate feedback (particles/sound) for exactly the face it changed.
2. **Errors are local, not global.** One bad connection or an
   over-limit device gets flagged on that device/face; it never takes
   the rest of a working network down.
3. **The energy/data split is invisible by default.** The player places
   one kind of wire and thinks of it as one thing; any future
   fine-grained control is an opt-in addition on top of the core, not
   part of it.
4. **Tool compatibility is tag-based** (a `c:wrenches`-style item tag),
   not a specific OC2R item — any mod's wrench works, addressed in the
   wrench-tool sub-project but the tag convention is decided here so
   later work doesn't have to guess.
5. **One source of truth for topology, updated strictly by event.** No
   state that can independently drift between client/server or across a
   save/load cycle — this is the single change responsible for closing
   out the "phantom cable" bug class.

## What's deliberately not decided here

- Whether any device type ever becomes explicitly shareable (e.g. a
  monitor visible to two computers) — plausible future work, not part
  of ownership's default exclusive model.
- The wrench item/recipe/tool-tag registration details — belongs to the
  wrench sub-project.
- Save-format migration for existing `BusCable`/`NetworkConnector`
  builds — its own sub-project; this doc only fixes the data model going
  forward (per-face override lives in the new block from the start).

---

pages.title: Device System
pages.body:
# Device System

OC2R has three layers for adding devices to a virtual computer. Each serves a different use case.

## VMDevice (low-level)

Registers memory-mapped IO (MMIO) regions and interrupt lines directly on the RISC-V board. The guest OS needs a kernel driver to use these devices.

**Lifecycle:**

1. `mount(VMTarget, VMContext)` — allocate resources, register MMIO and interrupts
2. `unmount()` — stop I/O, deregister
3. `dispose()` — free all resources

**Built-in implementations:**

| Device | Purpose |
|--------|---------|
| `DiskDriveDevice` | Floppy disk I/O |
| `HardDriveDevice` | Block storage |
| `KeyboardDevice` | Keyboard input |
| `MonitorDevice` | Framebuffer display |
| `NetworkInterfaceCardDevice` | Ethernet networking |
| `InternetCardDevice` | Internet connectivity |
| `NetworkTunnelDevice` | Network tunnel |
| `MemoryDevice` | RAM expansion |
| `PciCardCageDevice` | PCI device slot |
| `ProjectorDevice` | 3D projection |
| `FirmwareFlashStorageDevice` | Firmware storage |
| `SimpleFramebufferDevice` | Simple framebuffer |
| `PciRootPortDevice` | PCI root port |

## RPCDevice (high-level)

Communicates via JSON-RPC over a VirtIO serial port. No kernel driver needed — the guest runs a simple client that sends JSON method calls and receives JSON responses.

**Interface:**

```java
public interface RPCDevice {
    String getTypeName();
    List<RPCMethodGroup> getMethodGroups();
    Optional<RPCInvocation> getInvocation(RPCMethod method);
}
```

## ObjectDevice (@Callback)

A convenience implementation of `RPCDevice` using reflection. Annotate methods with `@Callback` and they are automatically exposed.

**Example:**

```java
public class MyDevice extends ObjectDevice implements NamedDevice {
    @Callback
    public double getTemperature() {
        return 36.6;
    }

    @Override
    public String getDeviceName() {
        return "Thermometer";
    }
}
```

**Available annotations:**

| Annotation | Usage |
|------------|-------|
| `@Callback` | Expose a method to the VM; supports `synchronize` (main thread), `name`, `description` |
| `@Parameter` | Describe a method parameter |

**Optional interfaces:**

| Interface | Purpose |
|-----------|---------|
| `NamedDevice` | Custom device name |
| `DocumentedDevice` | Extended documentation |
| `LifecycleAwareDevice` | Mount/unmount callbacks |

## FirmwareLoader

Special devices that provide boot firmware. The base interface adds `getFirmware()` returning a `Firmware` object (OpenSBI, Linux kernel, etc.). The lifecycle manager calls `load()` during initialization.

**Implementations:**

- `MinuxFirmware` — loads the `minux` kernel
- `ByteBufferFlashStorageDevice` — loads firmware from a byte buffer

## Device Bus Integration

Devices are exposed to the bus through **providers**:

```java
// BlockDeviceProvider — scan blocks for devices
public interface BlockDeviceProvider {
    void getDevices(BlockDeviceQuery query, List<Device> devices);
}

// ItemDeviceProvider — scan items for devices
public interface ItemDeviceProvider {
    void getDevices(ItemDeviceQuery query, List<Device> devices);
}
```

**Registration:**

Providers are registered via NeoForge `DeferredRegister` in `Providers.java`. Example item providers:

- `CPUItemDeviceProvider` — CPUs of various tiers
- `MemoryItemDeviceProvider` — RAM modules
- `HardDriveItemDeviceProvider` — storage drives
- `NetworkInterfaceCardItemDeviceProvider` — NIC
- `RedstoneInterfaceCardItemDeviceProvider` — redstone I/O

## Device Types

| Type | Tag | Example |
|------|-----|---------|
| `MEMORY` | `oc2r:devices/memory` | RAM stick |
| `HARD_DRIVE` | `oc2r:devices/hard_drive` | HDD/SSD |
| `FLASH_MEMORY` | `oc2r:devices/flash_memory` | BIOS/EEPROM |
| `CARD` | `oc2r:devices/card` | Network card |
| `CPU` | `oc2r:devices/cpu` | Processor |
| `ROBOT_MODULE` | `oc2r:devices/robot_module` | Robot upgrade |
| `FLOPPY` | `oc2r:devices/floppy` | Floppy disk |
| `NETWORK_TUNNEL` | `oc2r:devices/network_tunnel` | Tunnel card |

## Related

- [Architecture](https://github.com/DivByDiamond/OC2R/blob/39eb8109e2e38fdb047af98d8e6f7ded0194f498/docs/ARCHITECTURE.md) — device bus graph and VM lifecycle
- [Source Structure](https://github.com/DivByDiamond/OC2R/blob/39eb8109e2e38fdb047af98d8e6f7ded0194f498/docs/SRC_STRUCTURE.md) — code layout

---
